deep.reconstruction:
The page holds three blocks of notes, separated by rules. They look like a lecture or talk outline. Because of the pi list, the page is datable to about 1847 to 1853 (see block C).

A. Algebraic equations (keywords only; nothing is derived)
- 'Wurzeln. Gleiche Wurzeln in algebr. Gl. wie finden' means finding multiple roots of a polynomial P. The standard method is gcd(P, P'); I take that as the intended method, but it is not written.
- 'Zerlegung in Factoren' means factorisation of P into linear and quadratic factors, i.e. the fundamental theorem of algebra (FTA).
- 'Cauchys Beweis' refers to Cauchy's proof of the FTA (Cours d'analyse, 1821). It is a d'Alembert–Argand minimum-modulus argument: the minimum of |P| exists and must be 0.
- 'Insel in der Fig[ur] [der] Denks[chrift] nicht möglich' means 'an island in the figure of the Denkschrift is not possible'.
  - This most plausibly refers to the figure in Gauss's own 1799 dissertation proof of the FTA. That proof works with the curves Re P(x+iy)=0 and Im P(x+iy)=0. He revisited it in his 1849 jubilee paper.
  - The remark asserts that these curves have no closed component (an 'island') inside the circle.
  - My modern justification: u = Re P is harmonic. If u = 0 on a closed curve, the maximum principle forces u ≡ 0 inside it, which is impossible. Gauss's own justification is not on the page.

B. Trigonometric functions of an imaginary argument and the Gudermannian
In modern notation, with h = gd(x) (Gudermann's 'longitudo transcendens', Lambert's 'transcendent angle'):
- cos(ix) = (e^x + e^-x)/2 = cosh x = 1/cos h
- sin(ix) = (i/2)(e^x - e^-x) = i sinh x = i tan h
- tan(ix) = i(e^x - e^-x)/(e^x + e^-x) = i tanh x = i sin h
- Inverse: x = log tan(45° + h/2) = gd^{-1}(h), the Mercator-projection integral.

The next line, '... Arc. cos p+iq bestimmen = f - ig', announces the problem worked on the previous folio: find arccos of a complex number. From that folio:
- Write cos(f - ig) = p + iq. Then p = cos f cosh g and q = sin f sinh g.
- Put 1+p+iq = a e^{iA} and 1-p+iq = b e^{iB}.
- Since 1 + cos z = 2cos^2(z/2) and 1 - cos(conj z) = 2 sin^2(conj z /2):
  - sqrt(a/2) e^{±iA/2} = cos((f ∓ ig)/2)
  - sqrt(b/2) e^{±iB/2} = sin((f ± ig)/2)
- Taking moduli (my step): a = 2|cos((f-ig)/2)|^2 = cosh g + cos f and b = cosh g - cos f.
- Hence (a-b)/2 = cos f and (a+b)/2 = cosh g. So f = arccos((|1+w| - |1-w|)/2) and g = arccosh((|1+w| + |1-w|)/2), with w = p + iq.
- Multiplying the half-angle identities gives sqrt(ab) cos((A+B)/2) = sin f and i sqrt(ab) sin((A+B)/2) = sin(ig). The latter equals i sinh g, so sinh g = sqrt(ab) sin((A+B)/2). This provides a check and fixes the signs.
- Thus the page's Gudermannian table converts the hyperbolic quantities into ordinary trigonometric ones, suitable for logarithmic-trigonometric computation.

C. History of the computation of pi (number of decimals)
| Digits | Computer (Gauss's spelling) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| — | Archimedes | |
| 10 | Vieta (1593) | |
| 15 | Adrianus Romanus (1593) | used a polygon of 2^30 sides; Gauss writes 2^30 |
| 35 | Ludolf van Ceulen ('v. Cöln') | |
| 74 | Sharp (1699) | |
| 100 | Machin (1706) | |
| 127 | Lagny (1719) | |
| 140 | Vega (1789/94) | |
| 200 | Dase (1844) | |
| 208 | Rutherford (1841) | 'bloss 152 richtig', only 152 correct |
| 250 | Clausen (1847) | |
| — | 'Legend[re]' | presumably Legendre's 1794 proof of the irrationality of pi and pi^2 |

The list includes Clausen (1847) but omits Rutherford's 440 digits and Shanks (both 1853). This dates the page to about 1847 to 1853, consistent with Gauss's 1849 return to the 1799 Denkschrift.
errors: No mathematical errors in the Gudermannian relations; 1/cos h, i tg h, i sin h and x = log tg(45°+h/2) are all correct.
The arccos formulas on the previous folio are correct, though branch and sign choices (square roots, f in [0, pi], sign of g) are left implicit.

Historical figures, minor deviations from the modern record: Viète's value had 9 correct decimals; Sharp computed 72 digits (71 correct), not 74; Lagny's 127 had only 112 correct; Vega's 140 had 136 correct; Clausen's 250 had 248 correct. Gauss flags only Rutherford's error (152 correct), which matches the record.
'Insel ... nicht möglich' is stated without proof on this page.

deep.surprise_reason: These are lecture or outline notes. The Gudermannian relations and the complex-arccos formula were standard by the 1840s. The pi list is a routine historical summary, though it is a nice datable record of Gauss's awareness of Dase, Rutherford's error and Clausen. The remark that an 'island' in the 1799 figure is impossible is of mild interest for the history of the gap in his first FTA proof, but it carries no argument.

transcription_corrections: 'Insel in der Fign. [?] Denks. [?]' is best read as 'Insel in der Fig[ur] [der] Denks[chrift]', i.e. the figure of Gauss's 1799 FTA dissertation.
'Adrianus Rom. [?]' is Adrianus Romanus (Adriaan van Roomen); the '2^30' beside it is the number of polygon sides he used.
'Ludolf v. Colln' should be 'Ludolf v. Cöln' (Ludolph van Ceulen); the numeral 35 is written over another digit.
The word before 'Arc. cos' is uncertain ('Tum' is doubtful); the sense is 'determine arccos(p+iq) = f - ig', referring to the computation on the previous folio.
The numeral before 'Dase' appears to be corrected (overwritten) to 200.
